newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal's Gurkhas ask Britain for more pension.
newsitem.headline: Nepal's Gurkhas ask Britain for more pension.

text.p: Thousands of former Gurkha soldiers of the British Army organised a rally on Sunday demanding pensions and other benefits on a par with their British counterparts, organisers said.
Gurkhas, of Mongolian origin from the hills of Nepal, have served the British army for the past 180 years. About 232,000 Gurkhas fought under the British Crown in World War I and II.
British officials said more than 14,000 were killed and 28,000 were wounded in the two great wars, but ex-servicemen put the casualties much higher.

British officials said a 1947 treaty between Britain, India and Nepal laid conditions of service for the Gurkhas in the British or Indian armies "approximating" their basic pay to the Indian army's pay code.
But the Gurkhas have accused the British government of denying them equal benefits as provided for by the treaty.

Nicholas Soames, the British Armed Forces Minister, recently announced equal pay for Gurkha soldiers bringing them in line with their British counterparts. Gurkhas who had withdrawn from Hong Kong could also take their families to Britain.

But officials of the Gurkha Army Ex-Servicemen Organisation (GAESO), which is organising the protest, is also calling for pensions for Gurkha soldiers who retired in the late 1960s after service in Malaya, education and employment opportunities for their children and the right to live in Britain.
The rally, the first public protest since the Gurkhas started their agitation six months ago, was led by 80-year-old World War II veteran Lakshman Gurung, sitting in a wheel-chair.
"We Gurkhas ask: Do not discriminate against us. Give us the same pay and pensions as our British counterparts", read a banner raised at a meeting after the rally.
Another placard read: "War heroes with 15 pounds ($24) pension?"
Some 25,000 Gurkhas get British service pensions in Nepal.

Yubaraj Sangraula, GAESO's legal adviser, said the Gurkhas would take their case to British courts if their plight was not addressed by the British government by the end of April. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
